subtype: Approach: take the first offer accepted out of panic [Pitfall]
passage:
Jasleen: Kiran, you look tired. I thought you had started the new job?

Kiran: I did. In week two of being laid off I took the first offer that came.

Jasleen: Did you ask about the terms?

Kiran: No. I was scared of the gap. Lower pay than before, and the role isn't even what I trained for.

Jasleen: And now?

Kiran: Three months in and I am applying again. I've wasted the months and lost the pay.

Jasleen: Did you compare it with anything?

Kiran: No. I said yes to the first phone call. I'd have said yes to anything.

Jasleen: That's what fear does.

Kiran: I know. I should have asked for a day.

qa.q: How many months into the new job was Kiran when applying again?
qa.a: Kiran was three months into the job and applying again.

qa.q: What was Kiran feeling when accepting the first offer?
qa.a: Kiran felt scared of the gap without a job, and the fear made Kiran say yes without asking about terms.

qa.q: What could Kiran do differently with the next offer, and why?
qa.a: Kiran could ask for a day to read the terms and compare the role, because a short pause protects against a poor fit.

qa.q: How might Jasleen see Kiran's situation?
qa.a: Jasleen looks sympathetic and gently points out that fear made the decision, so probably feels concerned for Kiran.

grounding: Fearing the gap, an employee accepts a poorly paid, ill-fitting role without asking about terms and is looking again within three months.

subtype: Approach: take the first offer accepted out of panic [Pitfall]
passage:
I'm Anjali. I was laid off on a Monday in March, and by Thursday I had accepted a new job. I remember the relief. I didn't ask about hours, or the probation terms, or even what the role really involved. It paid ₹6,000 less, but I told myself a job is a job.
Keerthana, my closest friend from college, asked on the phone, 'Did you see the contract?' I said it was fine. I hadn't read it.
The role was night-shift data work, not the analytics I'd trained for. The contract said I couldn't leave for six months without paying back the joining costs. By May I was sleeping through the day, eating badly and applying to other jobs in secret on my phone.
Keerthana didn't say 'I told you.' She just helped me read the next offer properly, line by line.
I'm not angry at myself any more. I was scared. But the fear chose that job, not me.

qa.q: How much less did the new job pay?
What does 'the fear chose that job, not me' reveal about Anjali?
qa.a: Anjali sees that panic about the gap drove the choice, and now feels more forgiving than angry about it.

qa.q: What could Anjali have done before accepting on Thursday?
qa.a: Asked about the hours, role and probation terms and read the contract, perhaps with Keerthana, even if it took a few more days.

qa.q: How does Keerthana see Anjali's quick decision?
qa.a: Keerthana is worried from the start, asks about the contract, and later helps instead of blaming.

grounding: Shows an employee accepting a lower-paid, poorly fitting role out of fear of the gap and job-hunting again within three months.

subtype: Approach: take the first offer accepted out of panic [Pitfall]
passage:
Career counsellor's note, 3 June. Francis, alumni placement office.
Nandini first came to us in February, two days after her startup closed. She was shaking and said she'd take anything. I suggested she bring any offer to me before signing, but that week she accepted a sales role at a call centre, ₹5,000 below her old pay, without asking about targets or shift times.
Today she came back. The role has a monthly target she has never met, weekend shifts she didn't know about, and pay cuts for missed targets. She is job-hunting again, three months later, and more tired than before.
She said, 'I was so scared of an empty month that I didn't even ask what I was saying yes to.' She wasn't crying, but her voice was flat.
We went through two new openings together, with a list of questions to ask each one before any yes. I've booked a follow-up for next Friday.

qa.q: How much below her old pay was the sales role?
What does Nandini's flat voice suggest about how she feels?
qa.a: She seems worn out and disappointed in herself, still carrying the fear that pushed the first yes.

qa.q: What questions could help Nandini before the next yes?
qa.a: Questions about pay, targets, shift times, the actual work and any lock-in terms, compared against what she needs.

qa.q: How does the situation look to Francis, the counsellor who wrote the note?
qa.a: Francis sees a capable person pushed by fear into a poor fit, and responds with practical help and a follow-up rather than blame.

grounding: Shows an employee who, fearing the gap, took a lower-paid role without checking terms and was job-hunting again within three months.
